extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and readers of English constitutional and legal history
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the legal principles and limits governing the monarch's prerogatives, revenues, and ecclesiastical authority in English law, with historical statutory examples and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of judicial power from legislature and executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration of common justice must be in some degree separated both from the legislative and also from the executive power; uniting the provinces of a judge and a minister of state is to be avoided in a free constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If joined with the legislative, judges would become arbitrary and rule by opinion rather than by fundamental principles of law; if joined with the executive, it might overbalance the legislative. The statute 16 Car. I. c. 10 (abolishing the Star Chamber) removed judicial power from the king's privy council to prevent such abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial duty to follow fundamental principles of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are bound to observe fundamental principles of law even where legislators may depart from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between legislators (who may depart) and judges (who must observe); this underpins judicial independence and prevents arbitrary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's legal ubiquity in courts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the eye of the law the king is always present in all his courts though he cannot personally distribute justice; the regal office, not the royal person, is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: the king can never be nonsuit; in forms of proceedings the king is not said to appear 'by his attorney' as other men do; his judges reflect the king's image. (Footnotes: Fortescue, Co. Litt., Finch.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on royal proclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: The king's proclamations are binding when they are grounded upon and enforce the laws of the realm; they must not contradict old laws or tend to establish new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proclamations may govern manner, time, and circumstances of executing existing laws (example: proclamation laying embargo in time of war binding because founded upon prior law). But proclamations that assume dispensing power or legislate (e.g., allow papists arms or disarm Protestants) will not bind. Historical note: statute 31 Hen. VIII. c. 8 attempted to give proclamations force of acts of parliament but was later repealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal prerogative to confer honours and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: The king has sole power of conferring dignities, honours, knighthoods, peerages, and offices, on confidence that he will bestow them on those who deserve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles may be created by writs or letters patent or by investiture; offices and honours are convertible. Restriction: the king cannot create new offices with new fees annexed (that would be a tax on the subject requiring act of parliament). Example: letters patent creating an office with a new fee were voided in Parliament (13 Hen. IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative to grant private privileges and erect corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: The king may confer privileges on private persons (precedence, converting aliens to denizens) and erect corporations, granting them liberties, powers, and immunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded on the king's sole administration of government and his judgment as to capacities and distinctions best fitting service under the crown; historically carried far in imperial law (example: sacrilege to doubt prince's appointments).

rubrics_metrics.name: King as arbiter of domestic commerce and reference to law merchant
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic commerce is in part regulated by the lex mercatoria (law merchant); English law often refers causes of merchants to their peculiar customs and accepts merchant law in matters like bills of exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal laws alone cannot fully order trade between subjects of independent states; where merchant customs govern, English courts will refer to them (citations: Co. Litt., Ld Raym.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of markets and fairs by royal grant or prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: Public marts, markets and fairs (and tolls belonging thereto) can only be set up by virtue of the king's grant or by long immemorial usage and prescription which presupposes such a grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitation of times and places of markets is part of domestic polity (oeconomics) and falls within the king's prerogative as master of the realm. (Footnote: 2 Inst. 220.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation and custody of weights and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The prerogative of fixing a standard for weights and measures is vested in the crown; a visible material standard is necessary to reduce measures to uniform size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical standards (Winchester standard, Henry I's ulna/yard), statutes (compositio ulnarum et perticarum), derivation of other measures by multiplication/subdivision, standards kept in exchequer; parliamentary enactments attempted uniformity though custom resisted complete effect (citations: statutes and 2 Inst. 41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coinage: materials, impression, and denomination as royal prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Coining of money is the act of sovereign power; three considerations are materials (gold/silver historically), the impression (stamp), and the denomination (value) which are royal prerogatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically money of England must be gold or silver though copper coinage was later ordered (1672). Stamping/impression belonged to the crown (earlier mints by bishops/monasteries derived from royal grant). Denomination (value) is fixed by proclamation considering weight and fineness; king may legitimate foreign coin or decry domestic coin. Statute 25 Edw. III. c. 13 requires coin of sterling metal; whether the king can debase coin below or above sterling is contested in authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as head and supreme governor of the national church
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (26 Hen. VIII. c. 1 and 1 Eliz. c. 1) the king is the supreme head on earth of the Church of England and has annexed to the crown the titles, jurisdictions, authorities, and commodities of that dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In virtue of this the king convenes, prorogues, restrains, regulates, and dissolves convocations; convocation cannot make canons repugnant to the king's prerogative or laws without royal assent (statute 25 Hen. VIII. c. 19). The convocation's constitution resembles a miniature parliament (upper house bishops, lower house representative clergy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal nomination to ecclesiastical preferments and final ecclesiastical resort
rubrics_metrics.description: From the headship of the church arises the king's right of nomination to vacant bishopricks and certain ecclesiastical preferments; the king is the dernier resort in ecclesiastical causes with appeals ultimately to him in chancery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory bases: nomination by virtue of 25 Hen. VIII. c. 20; appeals restored to the crown by 25 Hen. VIII. c. 19; fuller treatment deferred to later chapters (contextual note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of king's revenue: ordinary vs extraordinary
rubrics_metrics.description: The king's revenue is either ordinary (subsisting time out of mind in the crown or granted by parliament by way of purchase/exchange) or extraordinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary revenue may be held in name of crown though many parts are in hands of subjects by grant; includes some revenues formerly thought absolute to the crown but granted away over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custody of temporalties of bishopricks during vacancy
rubrics_metrics.description: On vacancy of a bishoprick the custody of the temporalties (lay revenues, lands, tenements) reverts immediately to the king who has power to take intermediate profits and present to benefices during the vacancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: see considered founder of sees and to prevent spoil; statutes and charters (Henry I, Great Charter, statutes of Westminster, 14 Edw. III. st. 4. c. 4 & 5) limit abuses (waste, sale of custody). Historically kings kept sees long vacant to enjoy temporalties; modern custom usually returns temporalties to consecrated bishop intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corody (royal chaplain maintenance) entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is entitled to a corody out of every bishoprick — to have a chaplain maintained by the bishop or a pension until promotion to benefice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized as an acknowledgment to the king as founder of the see; said by some authorities to be due of common right though perhaps fallen into disuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to tithes in extraparochial places
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is entitled to all the tithes arising in extraparochial places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note expressed uncertainty whether this is strictly part of king's own royal revenue as these are held under implied trust for distribution for clergy's good; citation: 2 Inst. 647.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-fruits and tenths: origin, valuation, exemptions, and redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: First-fruits (primitiae/annates) and tenths (decimae) were annexed to the crown after papal claims were abolished; they are assessed by a valor and certain small livings are exempt or reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History: introduction by papal legates and opposition by parliament; statutes (26 Hen. VIII. c. 3; 1 Eliz. c. 4) annexed revenue to crown and established a new valor. Exemptions: vicarages under £10 and rectories under 10 marks discharged; payment scaling rules for incumbents of various durations; queen Anne's bounty (2 Ann. c. 11) vested revenues in trustees to augment poor livings — a statutory redistribution mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rents and profits of the demesne lands of the crown and limits on alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: Demesne lands (terrae dominicales regis) yield rents and profits; though much granted away, statute limits future grants and leases from the crown to terms no longer than 31 years or three lives (except houses up to 50 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where leases subsist, grants cannot create future interests exceeding the combined term limit. Tenants must be liable for waste and usual rent must be reserved, or where none, one third of clear yearly value. Historical loss of crown lands made the statute remedial but tardy (1 Ann. st. 1. c. 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military tenures, purveyance, and pre-emption — historic prerogatives and abolition
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown formerly enjoyed profits of military tenures and prerogatives of purveyance and pre-emption: buying provisions by purveyors at appraised valuation and impressing carriages/horses for royal service, often without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers were frequently abused and became oppressive; they declined and were finally resigned (at the Restoration Charles II ceded these powers in return for parliamentary settlement) with recompense by granting hereditary excise (e.g., fifteen pence per barrel on beer and ale). Military tenures were largely abolished by statute 12 Car. II. c. 24.
